warmup.q: The payments app keeps every payment in one file, one line per payment. To find a payment fast, it also keeps a lookup list: each payment's number, and where in the file its line starts. One night the lookup list is damaged and has to be deleted. What has the app lost?
options: Every payment made since the lookup list was last saved somewhere safe
Nothing it can't get back: read the file again and build a new list
The payments themselves, because the list was the only place that held their numbers
Only the payments that were being added to the list when it broke
warmup.why: The list holds nothing of its own. Every entry in it was worked out from a line in the file, so you can delete it and work it out again. That makes the list derived data, and the file the system of record, two ideas the second section builds up. Rebuilding takes a while, because it reads every payment once, and lookups are slow until it's done. But no payment is gone. The first and last options are the trap for anyone who thinks of the list as a second place where payments are stored: it only ever held copies of what the file says.

sections.h: One file of payments grows an index, a cache, a queue and a batch job
sections.html:
Let's build the program behind the card reader, the smallest version that could work. Before card readers, the café might have kept a notebook by the till, writing each sale on the next empty line and never rubbing one out. Our first program does the same with a file. Each time a card payment goes through, it adds one line to the end of a file called payments.log:

pay-0000001 m-cafe 2026-03-02 CAPTURED 47800

Each line is a record: one fact the program keeps. This one says that payment pay-0000001 paid 478.00 to the shop m-cafe on 2 March 2026, which is a lot of coffee. (The code calls a shop a merchant, so shop names start with m-.) Amounts are in cents, because whole numbers add up exactly and a computer's decimal fractions sometimes don't. CAPTURED means the money has really moved; the next section meets the step before it.

The payment number is the record's key, the value you look it up by. A crash or a restart wipes the program's memory, where it keeps its working data, but the file sits on disk and survives. A store that keeps its data through crashes is called durable.

For a week, this is enough. Then a customer calls to ask what happened to payment pay-0412233. The only way to find a line is to read the file from the top until it turns up. With a million payments the file is 46 MB, and finding the last one took 44 ms (thousandths of a second) in this lesson's demo. Say support staff and shop owners ask 200 questions like that every second. That's almost 9 seconds of reading for every second that passes, and the program can't keep up.

A thick notebook has the same problem, and the same fix: an index at the back. Read the file once, and note where each payment's line starts, counted in bytes (here, characters) from the top. Keep those positions in a map, a structure that stores a value under each key and finds it in one step. Now a lookup is one map access and one short read. It took about a microsecond (a millionth of a second) in the demo, tens of thousands of times faster than reading from the top.

That's an index: a lookup table from a key to where its record lives. Its price is memory for the map and a little extra work on every new payment. And after a restart the map is gone, so it must be built again from the file.

Next, shop owners get a screen that shows what they've taken today, which means adding up the shop's lines from today. Two thousand shops refresh it every 10 seconds, another 200 questions a second, and the answer rarely changes in between. So the program keeps each answer and hands it out until a new payment for that shop arrives. That's a cache: a saved copy of an answer that was costly to work out, like a sticky note by the till with today's total on it.

After each payment, the program also emails a receipt, and the email company sometimes takes 800 ms to reply. The customer at the till shouldn't wait for that. So the program writes a job, "send the receipt for pay-0000001", into a queue, a list of jobs waiting to be done, and answers the card reader at once. A separate program, called a worker, takes jobs off the queue and does them. If the email company is down for ten minutes, the jobs wait, and none is lost.

At night, the company pays each shop what it took that day, minus refunds and fees. One program reads all of yesterday's payments from start to end and writes one payout per shop. A program that works through a large, fixed pile of input in one run, usually on a schedule, is a batch job.

Put the pieces together and you have a data system: a few tools, each built for one kind of use, joined up by your own code. The figure shows ours. An app whose hardest problems are about its data (how much there is, how fast it changes, how to keep the copies in step) is called data-intensive. A payments app is one.

Some boxes in the figure hold facts, and some hold answers worked out from them. Next, we'll sort them, and that will explain the café's wrong balance.

try.title: Scan a file, then use an index
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It writes one million made-up payments to a temporary file, one line each. Then it finds the last one twice: once by reading the file from the top, and once through an index it builds in one pass over the file.
Predict before you run it: how many times faster will the index be? 10 times? 1,000? More?
Run it again with -Pargs=5000000 at the end of the command, for five million payments. Before you look, say which time will grow and which will stay about the same.

Here the file was already in memory, because the operating system (the program that runs all the others) keeps recently used files there, so a scan from the disk would be slower still. The Operating systems track explains how. Building the index costs one full scan too, once: that's the price of a restart.

aside.title: So where does a database fit in?
aside.html: A database is a program that stores records and answers questions about them, so you don't have to write the file handling yourself. Inside, it's built from the same pieces as our app. It adds each change to a log on disk before anything else, so a crash loses nothing. It keeps indexes, so a lookup doesn't read everything, and it keeps recently used data in memory, much like a cache. Starting from a plain file lets us see those pieces before a database hides them; the Storage engines track opens one up.

sections.h: Which data is the truth: systems of record and derived data
sections.html:
Look at the figure again and ask of each box: if it were deleted, could we get it back? The index: yes, read the log and build it again. The cache: yes, and it even refills itself as people ask. Last night's payouts: yes, run the batch job again over the same day of payments. The log: no. If payments.log is gone, nothing in the system knows that pay-0000001 ever happened.

That question splits all data into two kinds. A system of record, also called the source of truth, holds the official version of each fact. A new fact is written there first, and each fact appears there once. When anything else disagrees with it, the system of record is right by definition. Derived data is everything worked out from it: indexes, caches, totals, reports, even a fraud model (a program trained on old payments to spot suspicious new ones). It repeats the record on purpose, and can always be thrown away and worked out again.

The café's old notebook had the same split. The notebook was the system of record, and the index at the back and the sticky note by the till were derived. If coffee spilled on the note, the owner added up the notebook and wrote a new one. She'd never change the notebook to match the note.

The picture breaks at speed. She updated her note by hand, while our program updates its copies automatically, thousands of times a second. So the danger moves to an update that gets lost on the way.

Why keep copies at all? Each one reshapes the same facts to make one kind of question fast: by payment number, by shop and day, by card. The code calls such a copy a view. A stored answer like "money taken per shop per day" is a materialized view: the result of a question, kept so nobody has to work it out again.

Now we can explain the café's balance. Each card payment takes two records. When you tap your card, the shop first asks your bank to set the money aside, and the log gets an AUTHORIZED record. Later the money really moves to the shop, and the log gets CAPTURED. A refund adds REFUNDED.

Each new record also tells the cache to forget that shop's saved balance. The 40.00 refund reached the log, but that message was lost, so the cache kept handing out 49.00. It had gone stale: it missed the newest record. The log decides, so the balance is 9.00. The stepper below rebuilds all three views from the log.

Two habits keep this safe. Write the system of record first and the views second. Then a crash in between leaves a view behind the log, which a replay fixes, and never ahead of it. And keep the record complete and in its original order. Then any view can be rebuilt by reading the record from the start, which is called replaying it.

A copy that disagrees with the record is wrong. Rebuild it from the record. Do it now and then on purpose, too: if you've never rebuilt a view from scratch, you don't know that you can.

Any store can be the system of record; it depends on how the data flows. PostgreSQL, a popular database program, keeps records in tables, like rows in a spreadsheet. A payments table is the truth in one company and a read-only copy in another. And Kafka, a program that keeps named logs of messages called topics, can hold the truth that databases are built from. So of every store, ask: is this where a fact is decided, or a copy of it?

Rebuilding has a cost: it reads the whole record. Seven records take no time, but years of payments can take hours, and the view is missing until it's done. Keeping views in step as payments arrive is what much of this course is about. First, though, there's a kind of question that no index or cache makes fast. Next, we'll meet it.

try.title: Make a cache go stale, then rebuild
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It keeps a log of seven payment records and three views worked out from it (an index, daily totals and a cached balance), the same ones as in the stepper.
Before the refund, every view agrees with the log. Predict which view will be wrong after the refund whose cache message is lost, and by how much.
Read the last two lines of the code. The rebuild doesn't know what went wrong. Why does it fix the cache anyway?

code.title: RebuildDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: private fun record(e: Event, tellCache: Boolean = true) { log += e // 1. the log first applyToViews(e, tellCache) // 2. then every derived view } // ... six payments, then a refund whose cache message is lost: record(Event("pay-1", "m-cafe", "2026-03-03", "REFUNDED", 4000), tellCache = false) // drop every derived view and rebuild it from the log index.clear(); daily.clear(); balanceCache.clear() log.forEach { applyToViews(it) }

try.expect:
-- live views after 6 events
   index:  pay-1=CAPTURED pay-2=CAPTURED pay-3=CAPTURED
   daily:  m-cafe 03-02=4900 m-cafe 03-03=0 m-books 03-02=1250
   cache:  m-cafe balance=4900   (log says 4900)
-- after a refund the cache never heard about
   index:  pay-1=REFUNDED pay-2=CAPTURED pay-3=CAPTURED
   daily:  m-cafe 03-02=4900 m-cafe 03-03=-4000 m-books 03-02=1250
   cache:  m-cafe balance=4900   (log says 900)
-- all views dropped and rebuilt from 7 log records
   index:  pay-1=REFUNDED pay-2=CAPTURED pay-3=CAPTURED
   daily:  m-cafe 03-02=4900 m-cafe 03-03=-4000 m-books 03-02=1250
   cache:  m-cafe balance=900   (log says 900)

Amounts are in cents. After the lost message, the index and the totals are right and the cache is stale: 49.00 against a true 9.00. The rebuild needs no idea of what went wrong. It replays the 7 records, and every view, the cache included, agrees with the log again. The rebuilt cache starts empty and loads 900 on the first request.

Here are two questions about the same payments.

The card reader's program asks: did payment pay-0412233 go through? It asks thousands of times a second and needs the answer in a few milliseconds, because a customer is waiting. Each answer touches one record, found by its key through an index. The questions are fixed in advance, written into the app's code. Its writes are small too: add one payment, change one status.

An analyst, whose job is to find patterns in data, asks something else. What share of payments were refunded, for each kind of shop, week by week, over the last two years? She asks a few times a day, a little differently each time, and she's happy to wait seconds or minutes. The answer touches every payment from two years, maybe hundreds of millions of records. Yet it reads only three fields of each: the kind of shop, the week and whether the payment was refunded.

The first is operational work, usually called OLTP, online transaction processing. (Here a transaction means a business event such as a sale; the Transactions track gives the word its stricter meaning.) The second is analytical work, called OLAP, online analytical processing. They differ on almost every count:

Operational (OLTP) Analytical (OLAP)
Who asks the app's own code analysts and reports
Records per question one or a few, found by key millions, read one after another
Answer needed in milliseconds seconds to minutes
The questions fixed, written into the code new ones every day
The data describes how things are now everything that has happened
Writes one record at a time big loads, or a steady stream of events

Everyone first runs the analyst's question on the database the card readers use, and it breaks for a plain reason. The question reads every record, one after another, which is called a scan. While it runs, it competes with the card readers' lookups for the disk, memory and processor, and payments slow down for everybody.

The layout suits only one kind of work, too. Think of the café's notebook: each line holds one whole payment, with all its fields together. That's a row layout, and fetching one payment is one short read. But the analyst needs three fields from every line, and a row layout makes her read all the others too. An analytical store keeps all the values of one field together instead, like a separate notebook for each column. That's a column layout, and a scan reads only the columns it needs.

The Try it measures both. One lookup takes tens of nanoseconds (billionths of a second), and the analyst's question touches two million rows. Storing its three fields as columns makes it faster even in memory. On disk the gap is far larger, as the Storage engines track measures in Column stores and compression.

So the analyst's question has to leave the card readers' database. Next, we'll see where it goes.

try.title: One row against two million
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It builds two million made-up payments in memory twice: once as one object per payment (rows), and once as one array per field (columns).
Predict the ratio between the analyst's question and one lookup. A thousand times slower? A million?
Look at the two times for the analyst's question. Both read every payment. What does the column version not have to read?

code.title: TwoKindsDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: // operational: one payment, by its key val p = rows[1_234_567] // analytical: refund rate per category per week, every row for (r in rows) { // row layout: whole objects total[r.category][r.week]++ if (r.refunded) refunds[r.category][r.week]++ } for (i in 0 until N) { // column layout: three arrays total[categoryCol[i]][weekCol[i]]++ if (refundedCol[i]) refunds[categoryCol[i]][weekCol[i]]++ }

try.expect:
operational: payment 1234567 -> merchant 2382, 204.00, refunded=false
             1 row touched, about 42 ns per lookup (average of 100,000)
analytical:  refund rate per category per week, 8 categories x 104 weeks
             2,000,000 rows touched
             row layout    5.7 ms
             column layout 3.5 ms
             e.g. category 2, week 52: 4.7% of 2,405 payments refunded

The lookup time moved between about 20 and 60 ns (nanoseconds) over three runs on one laptop, and the scans moved by about 1 ms. The shape doesn't change: the analytical question does 2 million times the work of the operational one. Each row object here carries 17 fields, about 110 bytes, and the question needs 3 of them, 9 bytes per payment. The column layout reads only those bytes, which is why it wins even though everything is already in memory. A row store on disk has to read whole rows from the disk, so there the gap grows to many times this.

sections.h: Where the analytical copy lives: warehouses, lakes and lakehouses
sections.html:
So the analyst's work moves to its own copy of the data: derived data, like every view in the second section. Where that copy lives, and in what form, has had three answers.

The first, from the late 1980s and early 1990s, is the data warehouse: a separate database built for analytical questions. A payments company might run several programs with their own databases: payments, signing up new shops, fraud cases, customer support. The warehouse holds a read-only copy of all of them, reshaped into tables that suit analysis. Getting the data there is called ETL: extract it from each source, transform it into the warehouse's shape, and load it. So a warehouse is one huge materialized view of many systems of record, usually a few hours or a day behind them.

The second answer is the data lake. It began in the 2000s on groups of ordinary computers working together. From about 2015 it moved to cloud object storage: a service you rent over the internet, such as Amazon S3, that keeps files, called objects, by name, cheaply and safely. A lake holds files in any format: raw event records, spreadsheet exports, Parquet files (a file format that stores data by column), even images. Nothing checks their structure (which fields, of which types) when they're written; whoever reads them decides what they mean. That's cheap and flexible, and people who build models from data get the raw data a warehouse would have cleaned away.

A folder of files isn't a table, though. Two programs writing at once can leave a reader seeing half of an update. You can't change one row in place. And nobody can say which files make up the current version. Many companies ended up running both, a lake for raw data and a warehouse loaded from it: two copies that drift apart.

The third answer is the lakehouse, named in a 2021 paper by Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin and Zaharia: warehouse behaviour on lake storage. The data stays in Parquet files on object storage. A table format such as Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake adds small files that work like a contents page. They list exactly which data files make up each version of a table.

To change the table, a program writes its new data files first, then switches the table to a new contents page in one step that can't half happen. A reader sees the old version or the new one, never a mix. That brings back what the lake lost: all-or-nothing changes, a checked structure, and time travel (reading the table as it was yesterday). The Batch processing and analytics track builds one with Iceberg.

All three hold derived data; a payment is still decided in the operational systems they copy from. The Try it sorts a real company's stores by both of today's ideas.

try.title: Sort a payments company's stores
steps: For each store below, write two answers: system of record or derived, and operational or analytical.

1. The payments table in PostgreSQL that the card reader's program writes to. 2. Each shop's balance, saved for the balance screen in Redis, a program that keeps data in memory. 3. A search list that support staff use to find a payment by the last four digits of a card. 4. A copy of every payment, loaded each night into an Iceberg table for analysts. 5. A Kafka topic called payment-events that the payments program writes each event to first; the main database is built by reading it. 6. A fraud model trained on last year's disputed payments. 7. CSV files (plain text, one record per line, commas between the fields) of old payments that the finance team keeps in S3, in case they're ever needed.
For each one you marked derived, name the source you would rebuild it from.
try.expect:
1. The payments table: system of record, operational.
  2. The shop balances in Redis: derived, operational. They're rebuilt from the payments and serve the balance screen's quick reads.
  3. The search list: derived, operational. Delete it and you build it again from the payments table.
  4. The nightly Iceberg table: derived, analytical.
  5. The payment-events topic: system of record, because each event is written there first and the database is built from it. In a company that writes to the database first and copies the changes into a topic afterwards, the same topic would be derived. The role comes from the way the data flows, whatever the product.
  6. The fraud model: derived (from the old disputed payments), even though the app uses it on every new payment.
  7. The CSV files in S3: derived, analytical. They're a small, untidy data lake: nobody can say which files are current.

If you put the Redis balances under "system of record" because the balance screen reads only from them, look at the stepper again. Whatever the screen reads, those balances can be thrown away and rebuilt from the payments.

sections.h: How the rest of the course builds on this picture
sections.html:
Every later lesson zooms into part of this picture. The course has four parts.

Part Tracks The question it answers
I. Foundations What data systems are for (this track), Computer networking, Operating systems What do we ask of a data system, and how do the network and the operating system under it work?
II. Data on one machine The relational model and SQL; Data models beyond tables; Storage engines and query execution; Caching and in-memory data; Encoding, APIs and workflows How does one computer shape, store, find, cache and send its data?
III. Data across machines Replication; Partitioning; Transactions; Faults, time and truth; Consistency and consensus What changes when copies live on many computers, and each one can fail on its own?
IV. Moving and deriving data Messaging and logs; Stream processing; Batch processing and analytics; Derived data and doing right How does data flow from the records into every copy derived from them, and how do we keep the copies honest?

The rest of this track sets up the words the course uses to judge a design. Lesson 2 measures speed, and shows why the slowest 1 in 100 requests matters more than the average. Lessons 3 to 6 cover faults, load (the amount of work coming in), growing past one computer, and systems people can run and change for years.

Each lesson ends with a lab: a small working model of the idea that you finish yourself, with tests that tell you when it works. The networking and operating systems tracks come next: how computers send data to each other, and how a program gets help from the operating system. Every later lesson builds on both.

opening:
Picture a busy café. You tap your card to pay for a coffee, the card reader beeps, and you walk out. Somewhere, a program has written one line about that payment: which card paid, which shop, how much and when.

The next morning, the owner opens the café's app on her phone. It shows her balance, the money her card sales have brought in: 49.00. But she refunded a 40.00 order an hour ago, so the right balance is 9.00. Same app, same payments, two answers.

The tempting fix is to type 9.00 over the wrong number. It's the number everyone sees, so it feels like the real one. It's only a copy of the payments, though, and copies fall behind.

In this lesson, we'll build the program behind that card reader from one plain file. We'll find out which data is the record and which is a copy, and rebuild a broken copy. Then we'll meet the two kinds of questions people ask of data. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café owner whose app said 49.00 while its log of payments said 9.00. The log wins, because every other number in the app is a copy worked out from it, and a stale copy gets rebuilt, never typed over.

Next time you pay by card, open your bank's app. Look at the balance at the top and the list of payments under it. Ask which one is the record and which is worked out from it, and watch whether a new payment shows up in both at the same moment.

Next, we'll time the card reader's program, and find out why its average speed says so little about the customers who wait longest.

compare.title: The same payments, two kinds of question

a.label: Operational
a.title: the card reader's program, thousands of times a second
a.html: -- one row, found through an index on its key, in milliseconds SELECT status, amount_cents FROM payments WHERE payment_id = 'pay-0412233';

b.label: Analytical
b.title: an analyst, a few times a day
b.html: -- every payment from two years, three columns of each SELECT m.category, date_trunc('week', p.created_at) AS week, avg(CASE WHEN p.status = 'REFUNDED' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS refund_rate FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id WHERE p.created_at >= now() - interval '2 years' GROUP BY m.category, week ORDER BY week, m.category;

compare.note: Both questions are written in SQL, the language most databases understand. You don't need to read it yet; the SQL track teaches it. Both ask the same tables, and one database will run both. The shape of the work is what differs. The first follows an index to one row and answers in milliseconds. The second has to read every payment from two years, but only three of its columns, and its cost grows with the history. That's why it belongs on a copy laid out by column, such as a warehouse or lakehouse table, and not on the database the card readers are waiting for. In the second query, merchants is the table of shops. The Storage engines track shows why the two layouts differ.

worked.title: Rebuild a view from the log, by hand

steps.say: Start from the log: the seven records from the stepper, in order. Each line gives the record's position in the log (its offset), the payment, the shop, the day, what happened and the amount in cents. A view may use these records and nothing else.
steps.code:
0  pay-1  m-cafe   2026-03-02  AUTHORIZED  4000
1  pay-2  m-books  2026-03-02  AUTHORIZED  1250
2  pay-1  m-cafe   2026-03-02  CAPTURED    4000
3  pay-2  m-books  2026-03-02  CAPTURED    1250
4  pay-3  m-cafe   2026-03-02  AUTHORIZED   900
5  pay-3  m-cafe   2026-03-02  CAPTURED     900
6  pay-1  m-cafe   2026-03-03  REFUNDED    4000

steps.say: Name the question the view answers, because that decides its key. Daily totals answer "how much did shop m take on day d?", so the key is the pair (shop, day) and the value is the money taken, in cents. A HashMap holds one value per key.
steps.code: val totals = HashMap<Pair<String, String>, Long>() // (merchant, day) -> net cents

steps.say: Decide what each kind of record does to the view. An authorization only sets money aside on the card, so it changes nothing. A capture adds its amount on its own day. A refund takes its amount off on the day of the refund. merge adds the change to the total already stored for that key, or stores it if there is none.
steps.code: fun apply(e: Event) { val delta = when (e.kind) { "AUTHORIZED" -> return // reserves money, moves none "CAPTURED" -> e.cents // money moves on the capture's day "REFUNDED" -> -e.cents // and back on the refund's day else -> error("unknown kind ${e.kind}") } totals.merge(e.merchant to e.day, delta, Long::plus) }

steps.say: Rebuilding means: empty the view, then replay the log from offset 0, in order. Emptying it first is what makes it safe to run twice. Without that line, a second rebuild would count every payment twice.
steps.code: fun rebuild(log: List<Event>) { totals.clear() // start empty: safe to run twice for (e in log) apply(e) // offset 0 to the end, in order }

steps.say: Check it against the live view, the one kept up to date as payments arrived. Same records, same order, same rules: the same answer, every time. The café's total is 49.00 on 2 March and minus 40.00 on 3 March, the day of the refund.

lab.title: Rebuild every view from the log
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 10 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a TODO.

Read Log.kt. It's finished. PaymentEvent is one record, one line of the log. PaymentLog adds lines to a file and replays them in order. View is an interface, a list of functions that every view must have: apply folds in one more record, and clear empties the view. PaymentService writes to the log first and to the views second.
In Views.kt, write PaymentIndex.apply and get. An authorization creates the payment's entry. A capture or a refund changes only its status.
Write DailyTotals.apply and total: captures add, refunds subtract, and authorizations do nothing.

Write BalanceCache.get and apply. When the cache has no saved answer for a shop (a miss), call loader, the slow function that adds up the whole log, and count the load. A new record for a shop forgets that shop's saved balance, and no other.

Write rebuild, then run the tests until all 10 pass. One test file, RebuildPropertyTest, uses jqwik, a library that checks a rule against many random inputs. It tries 40 random payment histories, and if one breaks the rule, it shrinks it to the smallest history that still breaks it.
hints: byId[e.paymentId]?.let { byId[e.paymentId] = it.copy(status = e.kind) } updates an entry that's already there and ignores a payment number it has never seen.
totals.merge(e.merchant to e.day, delta, Long::plus) adds delta to the value already stored, or stores it if there is none.
cached.getOrPut(merchant) { loads++; loader(merchant) } runs the block only on a miss.
If rebuilding twice does not count anything twice fails, rebuild isn't emptying the views before it replays.

drill.title: Write rebuild from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write rebuild(log, views) for a log that can replay its records in order, and views that have apply and clear. Then write down the two things the log must promise for a rebuilt view to equal the live one.

answer.html: fun rebuild(log: PaymentLog, vararg views: View) { for (v in views) v.clear() // start empty, so running it twice is safe log.replay { _, e -> for (v in views) v.apply(e) } // every record, from offset 0, in log order } // 1. The log is complete: every fact that reached any view is in it. // (So write the log first and the views second.) // 2. Its order never changes: a refund replayed before its capture // would leave the payment CAPTURED.

recap: A data system is a few tools joined up by your code: a file or database keeps the records, an index finds one fast, a cache keeps answers that are costly to work out, a queue holds jobs for later and a batch job works through a big pile at once.
The system of record holds each fact once and wins every disagreement. Everything worked out from it (indexes, caches, totals, warehouses, models) is derived data, and can be thrown away and rebuilt.

Write the record first and the copies second, and keep the record complete and in order. Then any copy can be dropped and replayed, and a copy that disagrees with the record gets rebuilt, never patched.

Operational work touches a few records by key, in milliseconds, for the app. Analytical work scans millions of records, in seconds or minutes, for people asking new questions, and it belongs on its own copy.

Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses are three homes for that analytical copy: a separate database, files on cheap cloud storage, or those files plus a table format that adds versions and all-or-nothing changes.

The limit: a rebuild reads the whole record. Seven records take no time, but years of payments can take hours, and the copy is missing until it's done. Keeping copies in step as payments arrive is what much of this course is about.

explain.prompt: A friend who's new to programming sees that the payments app keeps the same payments in four places: the payment log, a cache for the balance screen, a search list for support staff and a warehouse for analysts. They ask whether that's asking for trouble. Explain it to them in your own words.
explain.answer: Only one of the four is the truth. The payment log is the system of record: every payment is written there first, once, and it wins any argument. The other three are copies worked out from it, each shaped for one kind of question. The cache answers "what's my balance?" in a moment, the search list lets support staff find a payment by the last digits of a card, and the warehouse lets analysts read two years of history without slowing the card readers down. The trouble is real: a copy can fall behind or be wrong. The app handles it by always writing the log first, keeping it complete and in order, and treating every copy as something it can throw away. When a copy disagrees with the log, you fix the cause and rebuild the copy from the log, never the other way round.

deeper.html:
One size doesn't fit all. In 2005, Michael Stonebraker and Uğur Çetintemel argued in a paper at ICDE, a database research conference, "One Size Fits All: An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone", that one general-purpose database can't serve every kind of work well, and that specialized programs (for analysis, for streams of events, for search) would win in their niches. Twenty years on, that's the usual design: one system of record and several specialized derived stores. The cost is the one this lesson names, keeping them in step, and Part IV of this course is about paying it well.

Where lakes began. The first data lakes ran on Hadoop, free software for storing and processing files across many computers, which grew out of papers Google published about its own systems. The Batch processing and analytics track tells that story and shows what survived of it.

ETL or ELT. When the transform step runs inside the warehouse, after the raw data has been loaded, the process is called ELT: extract, load, transform. It became common once cloud warehouses grew cheap and fast, partly because the raw data stays there to transform again if the first transform had a bug.

Both kinds of work in one system. Some products, called HTAP (hybrid transactional and analytical processing), run both kinds of work in one system, usually with two parts inside: one that keeps rows for lookups and one that keeps columns for scans. They suit cases such as a fraud check that needs totals over very fresh data. They don't remove the need for a separate analytical copy, because a company has many operational databases and wants one place to analyze them all together.

A third kind of work. Some analytical questions now run inside the app itself: a shop's screen that shows its payments per minute over the last 90 days, updated as payments arrive. Databases built for this, such as Apache Pinot, Apache Druid and ClickHouse, take in events as they happen and answer such totals in tens of milliseconds. Classic warehouses, built for big loads and long scans, don't. The Batch processing and analytics track compares them.

Data flows back too. Results of analysis often return to the operational side. A fraud model trained in the warehouse scores live payments, and a risk rating for each shop, worked out overnight, is copied into the database the card readers use. Copying warehouse results back into operational stores is sometimes called reverse ETL. It's still derived data, flowing the other way, and it needs the same care: a stale risk rating is a stale cache.

Many readers, one lakehouse table. Because a lakehouse table is data files and metadata in formats that any program may read and write, several programs can query the same table. Among them are Spark (which runs big data jobs across many computers), Trino (which runs SQL over files in object storage) and DuckDB (a small database that runs inside another program).

The framing of operational versus analytical systems, and of systems of record versus derived data, follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 1, which goes on to cloud versus self-hosted systems and to distributed versus single-machine designs (lesson 5 of this track).
